title: Engagement Ring Settings Explained: Solitaire, Halo, Hidden Halo, Trilogy and More
teaser: Discover the most popular engagement ring settings and what makes each one unique.
body:
The setting of an engagement ring changes everything. It shapes the overall style, influences how the diamond is seen, and affects how the ring feels in everyday wear. Even the same centre stone can look completely different depending on the setting around it.

A solitaire is the most classic option. It places the focus entirely on the centre diamond, with minimal distraction. Clean, timeless and elegant, it suits buyers who want simplicity and longevity.

A halo setting surrounds the centre stone with smaller diamonds. This can increase sparkle and create the impression of a larger centre diamond. Halo rings often feel more decorative and romantic, particularly in vintage-inspired designs.

A hidden halo offers a subtler version of that detail. The smaller diamonds sit just beneath the centre stone rather than around the top view. From above, the ring still appears refined and minimal, but from the side there is an added layer of light and craftsmanship.

A trilogy ring features three stones, often symbolising past, present and future. It has emotional resonance as well as visual presence, and it works beautifully for those who want more substance than a single-stone design.

Other setting details matter too. Pavé bands add delicate sparkle. Bezel settings create a sleek, modern edge and offer extra security. Cathedral shoulders lift the centre stone for a more dramatic profile.

The best setting depends on what you want the ring to express. Do you want restraint or brilliance? Minimalism or detail? Traditional structure or modern softness? The centre diamond may be the heart of the ring, but the setting is what gives it its language.

title: How to Care for Diamond Jewellery So It Keeps Its Sparkle
teaser: Keep your diamond jewellery shining brilliantly with simple care tips.
body:
Diamond jewellery is made to be worn and enjoyed, but regular wear naturally leads to buildup from lotion, soap, oils and everyday dust. Over time, that buildup can dull the surface of a diamond and reduce the brightness that makes it so beautiful. The good news is that a little care goes a long way.

The simplest habit is regular gentle cleaning. Warm water, mild soap and a very soft brush are often enough to remove everyday residue. After cleaning, rinse thoroughly and dry with a soft lint-free cloth. This can help restore the sparkle that often fades simply because the stone is no longer completely clean.

Storage matters as well. Jewellery should be stored carefully to avoid scratching or tangling. Individual pouches or lined boxes help protect each piece, especially rings, bracelets and earrings with fine metalwork.

It is also worth paying attention to when you wear your jewellery. While diamonds are extremely hard, settings and metal can still be affected by impact, chemicals or rough activity. Removing pieces before cleaning, heavy exercise or hands-on tasks can help preserve them over time.

For fine jewellery worn often, occasional professional checks are important. Prongs, clasps and settings can loosen gradually without being obvious at first. Having them inspected helps prevent unnecessary damage or stone loss.

A diamond does not lose its beauty with wear. But like anything precious, it responds well to care. With the right habits, your jewellery will continue to look polished, bright and effortless for years to come.

title: How to Choose the Right Carat Weight Without Overpaying
teaser: Find the perfect diamond size while staying within your budget.
body:
Carat weight is one of the first things people notice when buying a diamond, but it is also one of the easiest things to misunderstand. Carat measures a diamond’s weight, not its exact visual size. That distinction matters, because two diamonds with the same carat weight can look quite different once set.

A well-proportioned diamond can appear larger and brighter than a poorly cut stone of the same weight. Shape also changes visual impact. Oval, pear and marquise diamonds often appear larger face-up than round diamonds of the same carat weight because of their elongated outlines.

Choosing the right carat weight is really about understanding what look you want. Some people want finger coverage and presence. Others prefer subtlety and balance. A diamond does not need to be large to feel luxurious. In many cases, the overall proportions of the stone and the design of the setting do just as much work as the carat number itself.

It can also help to think practically. Certain carat thresholds often attract a noticeable jump in price, even when the visual difference is minimal. Choosing just below one of those points can sometimes offer better value while giving a very similar appearance.

The smartest way to buy is to decide on your priorities first. Are you aiming for maximum size? Strong sparkle? A clean, refined everyday look? Once that is clear, carat becomes one part of the decision rather than the only one.

At DIAMA, we encourage a balanced approach. The best diamond is not simply the heaviest one. It is the one that looks right, feels right and makes sense for the piece you are choosing.

title: The 4Cs of Diamonds
teaser: Cut, Colour, Clarity and Carat Made Simple
body:
If you are shopping for a diamond, the first thing you will keep seeing is the 4Cs: cut, colour, clarity and carat. These are the standard quality factors used to evaluate diamonds, and they give you a practical way to understand how a stone will look, why it is priced the way it is, and where it may be worth compromising.

1. Cut: how well the diamond handles light

Cut is often the most important of the 4Cs because it has the biggest effect on sparkle. A well-cut diamond reflects light back to the eye more effectively, which is what gives it brightness, fire and life. The cut grades for most diamonds are:

1)       Excellent

2)       Very Good

3)       Good

4)       Fair

5)       Poor

In simple terms, Excellent cut diamonds are the most lively and bright, while Poor cut diamonds can look dull because light escapes rather than returning to the viewer. This is why cut can matter more visually than chasing the highest possible clarity or colour grade on paper.

2. Colour: how white the diamond appears

Diamond colour grading for white diamonds runs from D to Z.

D represents the most colourless end of the scale, while grades further down the alphabet show increasing traces of yellow or brown.

We can divide this scale into five broad groupings:

1)       D–F Colourless

2)       G–J Near Colourless

3)       K–M Faint

4)       N–R Very Light

5)       S–Z Light

For many buyers, the most useful thing to know is that you do not always need the very top colour grade for a diamond to look beautiful. A well-cut stone in the near-colourless range can still appear bright and refined, especially once set into jewellery.

3. Clarity: how visible the internal characteristics are

Clarity refers to the presence of internal features and surface blemishes, assessed under 10x magnification.

There are 11 grades:

1.       FL – Flawless

2.       IF – Internally Flawness

3.       VVS1 – Very Very Slighly Included 1

4.       VVS2 – Very Very Slighly Included 2

5.       VS1 – Very Slighly Included 1

6.       VS2 – Very Slighly Included 2

7.       SI1 – Slighly Included 1

8.       SI2 – Slighly Included 2

9.       I1 – Included 1

10.  I2 – Included 2

11.  I3 – Included 3

These stand for Flawless, Internally Flawless, Very Very Slightly Included, Very Slightly Included, Slightly Included, and Included.

At the top of the scale, FL means no inclusions or blemishes are visible to a skilled grader at 10x magnification. At the lower end, I1 to I3 means inclusions are obvious under magnification and may affect transparency, brilliance, or durability. Most diamonds fall somewhere in the middle, commonly in the VS or SI ranges.

For most shoppers, the practical goal is not perfection. It is finding a diamond that looks clean to the eye and still offers good value.

4. Carat: the weight of the diamond

Carat is different from the other Cs because it is not a named grade like Excellent or VS1. It is a measurement of weight. One metric carat equals 200 milligrams, and each carat is divided into 100 points. That means a 0.50 carat diamond is also 50 points, and a 1.25 carat diamond is 125 points.

This is important because carat tells you how much a diamond weighs, not exactly how large it will look. Two diamonds with the same carat weight can face up differently depending on their cut and shape. That is why carat should always be considered alongside the other 3Cs rather than on its own.

The 4Cs work together

The best diamond is rarely the one with the highest grade in every category. A balanced combination usually matters more. A slightly lower colour or clarity grade can still look exceptional if the cut is strong and the diamond presents beautifully in real life. The aim is not to buy the most technical perfection on paper. The aim is to choose a stone that looks beautiful, suits your priorities, and feels right for the piece you are buying.

For a customer, understanding the 4Cs makes the buying process much clearer. It gives context to the certificate, helps separate what matters visually from what matters only on paper, and makes it easier to choose with confidence.
